Abstract
Purpose  To develop and validate a hybrid radiomics model to predict the overall survival in pancreatic cancer 
patients and identify risk factors that affect patient prognosis.
Methods  We conducted a retrospective analysis of 272 pancreatic cancer patients diagnosed at the First Affiliated 
Hospital of Soochow University from January 2013 to December 2023, and divided them into a training set and a 
test set at a ratio of 7:3. Pre-treatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging 
(MRI) images, and clinical features were collected. Dimensionality reduction was performed on the radiomics features 
using principal component analysis (PCA), and important features with non-zero coefficients were selected using 
the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) with 10-fold cross-validation. In the training set, we built 
clinical prediction models using both random survival forests (RSF) and traditional Cox regression analysis. These 
models included a radiomics model based on contrast-enhanced CT, a radiomics model based on MRI, a clinical 
model, 3 bimodal models combining two types of features, and a multimodal model combining radiomics features 
with clinical features. Model performance evaluation in the test set was based on two dimensions: discrimination and 
calibration. In addition, risk stratification was performed in the test set based on predicted risk scores to evaluate the 
model’s prognostic utility.
Results  The RSF-based hybrid model performed best with a C-index of 0.807 and a Brier score of 0.101, 
outperforming the COX hybrid model (C-index of 0.726 and a Brier score of 0.145) and other unimodal and bimodal 
models. The SurvSHAP(t) plot highlighted CA125 as the most important variable. In the test set, patients were 
stratified into high- and low-risk groups based on the predicted risk scores, and Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated 
a significant survival difference between the two groups (p < 0.0001).
Conclusion  A multi-modal model using radiomics based on clinical tabular data and contrast-enhanced CT and MRI 
was developed by RSF, presenting strengths in predicting prognosis in pancreatic cancer patients.

Introduction
Pancreatic cancer is a malignant tumor with poor prog­
nosis and high mortality. Due to the lack of typical clini­
cal manifestations and effective diagnostic methods, 
most patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage, and 
the overall 5-year relative survival rate is about 12% [1]. 
Early detection of pancreatic cancer is critically impor­
tant, as diagnosis at a resectable stage significantly 
improves the likelihood of long-term survival. How­
ever, current screening and diagnostic strategies remain 
inadequate, underscoring an urgent need for novel and 
sensitive approaches to identify pancreatic cancer at an 
earlier stage [2, 3]. Although recent advances in surgi­
cal techniques, adjuvant, and neoadjuvant therapies 
have improved clinical management, the overall long-
term survival rate remains unsatisfactory [4]. In order to 
explore the risk factors affecting the prognosis of pancre­
atic cancer patients and guide the selection of individual­
ized treatment plans, predicting the clinical outcomes of 
pancreatic cancer patients is particularly important.
With the advancement of pancreatic cancer research, 
an increasing number of factors have been identified as 
being associated with the survival prognosis of patients. 
Moreover, various prediction models now incorporate 
more variables such as serum indicators, imaging data, 
and pathology data into prognostic scoring system. This 
enables the development of a more comprehensive pre­
diction model for evaluating the survival prognosis of 
pancreatic cancer patients. Keyl et al. [5] established a 
prognostic model based on factors including age, CA199, 
C-reactive protein, metastatic status, neutrophil-to-lym­
phocyte ratio and total serum protein level to stratify 
patients with different prognostic risks, and this model 
has a favourable prediction performance.
Owing to the pancreatic gland’s status as a retroperi­
toneal organ, situated at a deep level with adjacency to 
essential blood vessels and nerves, the intricate nature of 
the peri-pancreatic anatomy complicates the undertaking 
of preoperative biopsies. In the clinical setting, imaging 
techniques exhibit distinct advantages, offering crucial 
parameters, e.g., tumor dimensions, vascularity and the 
degree of peritumoral infiltration.
However, the traditional imaging diagnosis relies heav­
ily on the physician’s experience and subjective inter­
pretation, and has certain limitations for quantitative 
assessment of subtle features, internal structure, and 
functional status. Radiomics is a novel method to image 
analysis that automatically extracts numerous quantita­
tive features in high throughput from standard medical 
imaging [6]. These quantitative imaging features can be 
used to establish prognostic models and stratify patients 
based on different clinical outcomes (such as overall sur­
vival, progression-free survival, etc.) [7], and radiomics 
has already found broad applications in oncology practice 
[8–10]. A number of studies have shown that radiomics 
can be used for the diagnosis [11–13], staging and grad­
ing [14, 15], prognostic prediction [16–18], and efficacy 
evaluation [19–22] of pancreatic cancer. However, these 
studies are limited by their reliance on single-modality 
CT or MRI imaging, which may not fully capture the 
complexity of tumor biology processes. To increase the 
informational content of medical images and achieve 
more accurate prognostic prediction models, the trend 
is shifting towards constructing multimodal prognostic 
models that combine various types of imaging features.
In this study, our objective is to establish a comprehen­
sive model predicting the prognosis of pancreatic cancer 
patients by integrating baseline radiomics features and 
clinical characteristics. This model seeks to provide a reli­
able reference for clinical treatment and enhance patient 
survival rates.
Materials and methods
Patients
This retrospective study has been approved by the Insti­
tutional Review Board of our institution. A total of 272 
pancreatic cancer patients diagnosed between 2013 and 
2023 at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow Univer­
sity were included in this study. The training and testing 
sets were randomly divided from the enrolled patients at 
a ratio of 7:3. Inclusion criteria were: (1) Pancreatic can­
cer confirmed by pathological diagnosis; (2) Abdominal 
contrast-enhanced CT and MRI examinations performed 
at our hospital before define treatment. Exclusion criteria 
were: (1) Lack complete contrast-enhanced CT and MRI 
scan sequences; (2) Poor quality of contrast-enhanced 
CT and MRI imaging; (3) Combined with a history of 
other malignant tumors; (4) Lack complete clinical data 
or follow-up data. Patients were randomly divided into a 
training set (n = 190) and a test set (n = 82) at a ratio of 
7:3. The process of case selection is illustrated in Fig. 1.
Clinical data and follow-up
The included patients were evaluated by a multidisci­
plinary team consisting of oncologists and radiologists. 
Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI images prior to treat­
ment were collected for 272 patients, along with clinical 
parameters extracted from the electronic medical record 
system, including gender, age, clinical staging, and labo­
ratory test results from the first hospital admission (com­
plete blood count, liver function, renal function, tumor 
markers, etc.). The 8th edition of the American Joint

Committee on Cancer (AJCC) was used to assess the 
clinical staging of the tumors [23]. All patients were fol­
lowed up through telephone calls and hospital visits until 
mortality, with the follow-up cut-off date being January 1, 
2024. Follow-up data included the overall survival (OS) 
of the patients, defined as the time from the initial patho­
logic diagnosis to mortality from any cause or to the last 
known date of survival.
Image acquisition
All patients underwent contrast-enhanced CT and MRI 
scans prior to treatment. The examination equipment 
comprised a 256-slice CT scanner (GE Revolution CT, 
GE, USA) and a PhilipsIngenia 3.0T magnetic reso­
nance imaging (MRI) system equipped with a 32-channel 
abdominal phased-array coil. Prior to the examination, 
patients were instructed to fast and abstain from water 
intake for 6 h, in addition to undergoing breath-hold 
training. CT scanning parameters were as follows: tube 
voltage of 120 kVp, tube current of 200 to 450 mAs, 
pitch of 0.992, slice thickness and interslice gap both 
set at 5 mm, an image matrix of 400 × 400 pixels, and 
reconstructed slice thickness of 1.25 mm. For contrast-
enhanced scans, iodixanol 320 was used as the contrast 
agent, administered at a dosage of approximately 1.4 
ml/kg body weight at an injection rate of 3 ml/s. Auto­
matic triggering was employed to acquire arterial phase 
images following contrast injection, with a threshold trig­
ger value set at 100 Hounsfield Units (HU), followed by 
acquisition of venous phase images after a delay of 30 s. 
MRI scanning parameters for the axial fat-suppressed 
T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) sequence were: repetition 
time (TR) of 448 milliseconds, echo time (TE) of 70 mil­
liseconds, flip angle (FA) of 90 degrees, and a matrix size 
of 228 × 199.
Region of interest and segmentation
DICOM format images of Contrast-enhanced CT images 
during the portal venous phase and MRI axial fat-
suppressed T2-weighted sequences were selected and 
imported into 3D Slicer software version 5.6.1. Under 
the guidance of a radiation oncology physician with 20 
years of experience, two radiation oncology physicians 
delineated the regions of interest (ROIs) layer by layer

along the contours of the cancer lesions on the CT and 
MRI images, taking care to avoid surrounding blood ves­

images and were blinded to the clinical outcomes before 
the ROI segmentation. In cases of significant discrepan­

with 20 years of experience made the final decision based 
on NCCN (National Comprehensive Cancer Network) 
guideline [24]. To evaluate the consistency and reliabil­
ity of ROI delineation between the two physicians, 90 
patients were randomly selected for inter-observer agree­
ment analysis using the intraclass correlation coefficient 
(ICC). The processing flow of image and clinical data is 
shown in Fig. 2.
Extraction of radiomic features
Prior to feature extraction, images were resampled using 
the 3D Slicer software to a voxel size of 3*3*3 mm³ to 
achieve isotropy, thereby minimizing variability due to 
scanning equipment and protocols. Radiomic features 
were then extracted using the Radiomics plugin within 
the 3D Slicer software. A total of 1037 features were 
extracted, including 108 original features and 929 filter 
(Laplacian of Gaussian, LoG; wavelet) features, catego­
rized into seven types: shape features, first order (FO) 
features, features based on gray-level cooccurrence 
matrices (GLCM), gray level dependence matrix (GLDM) 
features, features based on run length matrices (RLM), 
features based on size zone matrices (SZM), and fea­
tures based on neighborhood gray tone difference matri­
ces (NGTDM). To eliminate differences in feature scales 
and improve model convergence, all extracted radiomic 
features were standardized using z-score normalization 
before further analysis.
The development and evaluation of models
The extracted radiomics features were subjected to 
data dimensionality reduction by principal component 
analysis (PCA). Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selec­
tion Operator (LASSO) Cox regression and 10-fold 
cross-validation were applied to the dimensionality 
reduced radiomics features, clinical features, and com­
bined features (CT + clinical, MRI + clinical, CT + MRI 
and CT + MRI + clinical features), respectively, to select 
the significant features with non-zero coefficients. In 
the training set, the following models were constructed 
by random survival forest (RSF) and traditional Cox 
regression algorithms using the selected features: a clini­
cal model, a CT-based radiomics model, an MRI-based 
radiomics model, and “bimodal” models of CT + MRI, 
CT + clinical, and MRI + clinical, and finally a hybrid

model combining all the features. Finally, a hybrid model 
is built by combining all the features.
We used the scaled Schoenfeld residual test to check 
the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. The Brier 
score was utilized to compare the consistency between 
the predicted and observed OS, serving as a measure to 
evaluate the model’s prediction accuracy. The discrimi­
nation of the models was assessed using the C-index. 
Furthermore, we plotted dual-axis charts showing how 
Brier score and AUC change over time to evaluate model 
performance. To compare the predictive ability of dif­
ferent models more rigorously, we conducted pairwise 
comparisons of C-index values using a bootstrap resam­
pling method (n = 500), with p-values adjusted using the 
Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Statistical significance 
was defined as an adjusted p-value < 0.05.
To enhance the clinical applicability of the model, we 
performed risk stratification based on predicted risk 
scores in the test set. The optimal cutoff value was deter­
mined using a statistical approach that identifies the 
threshold which maximizes the difference in survival 
outcomes between groups, based on log-rank statistics. 
Patients were then classified into high-risk and low-risk 
groups for further survival comparison.
Statistical analysis
The difference of demographic and clinical information 
between the training set and the test set was evaluated 
using SPSS 26. The normality of continuous variables was 
assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Normal-
distributed continuous data were subjected to indepen­
dent samples t-tests for analysis, whereas non-normal 
distributed continuous data were examined through 
Mann-Whitney U tests. Categorical variables were sys­
tematically evaluated using contingency tables and chi-
square tests for statistical evaluation. The p values less 
than 0.05 were believed to be statistically significant.
The feature selection, model construction, and model 
evaluation were performed in R software (version 4.3.2). 
The “glmnet” package was used to perform LASSO logis­
tic regression. The “randomForestSRC” and “survival” 
packages were used for model construction. Additionally, 
the “surv_cutpoint” function from the “survminer” pack­
age was applied to determine the optimal cutoff value for 
risk stratification based on maximized log-rank statistics.
Result
The characteristics of patients
A total of 272 patients were included in the study: 190 in 
the training set and 82 in the test set. The detailed clinical 
information was summarized in Table 1. The median fol­
low-up period in the training and test sets were 16.32 and 
17 months, respectively. A total of 116(61.1%) patients 
and 52(63.4%) patients were confirmed dead in the train­
ing and test sets during the follow-up period. All features 
demonstrate no significant differences between the train­
ing set and the test set.
The development of models

CT imaging radiomic features and 1037 MRI imag­
ing radiomic features as well as 18 clinical features were 
extracted. To assess inter-observer consistency in tumor 
segmentation, ICC analysis was performed on 90 ran­
domly selected patients. The average ICC value was 0.881 
for CT-based features and 0.906 for MRI-based features, 
indicating good reproducibility. Feature-wise ICC values

(PCA) was applied to dimensionality reduction of the CT 
and MRI imaging radiomic features, and the top 18 CT 
principal components and the top 15 MRI principal com­
ponents were retained as the dimensionality-reduced fea­
tures because they were able to cumulatively explain 80% 
of the total variance of the dataset. We chose 80% as the 
threshold because it is a widely recognized criterion in 
the previous literature [25], aiming to ensure maximum 
information retention yet effective data dimensionality 
reduction. Fig. S2 shows how the cumulative explained 
variance varies with principal components. Subsequently, 
we used the least absolute shrinkage and selection opera­
tor (LASSO) Cox regression to retain features with non-
zero coefficients, determined the optimal regularization 
parameter λ value through 10-fold cross-validation to 
exclude redundant features, and screened 7 CT features, 
6 MRI features, 9 clinical features, 12 CT + clinical fea­
tures, 7 MRI + clinical features, 4 CT + MRI features, and 
9 hybrid features (CT + MRI + clinical features). Fig. S3 
demonstrates the process of feature screening. Figure 3 
using hybrid features as an example, shows the coefficient 
path plot and cross-validation curve for feature selection 
with LASSO. The selected features are used to construct 
the prediction models based on RSF and traditional Cox 
regression, respectively. Prior to modeling, we performed 
a collinearity diagnostics using the correlation coefficient 
matrix. Taking the hybrid model as an example, we plot­
ted a heatmap of the correlation coefficient matrix (Fig. 
S4), and the results showed that there was no collinearity 
issue among the features.
Using grid search to select the significant parameters 
for Random Survival Forest and establishing the RSF-
based model, the optimal structure of the RSF model 
comprised 500 estimators, 10 minimum of samples split, 
and 10 minimum of samples leaf. Figure 4 presents a 
visualization of the RSF algorithm.
Incorporating features extracted by LASSO into Cox 
multivariate regression, taking the hybrid model as an 
example, the forest plot (Fig. 5) reveals that the nine 
incorporated variables each serve as independent prog­
nostic factor. The Schoenfeld residuals was utilized to 
examine the proportional hazards (PH) assumption for 
the variables identified through LASSO. The results show 
that all variables in Cox-based hybrid models satisfied 
the PH assumption (p > 0.05). Figure 6 demonstrates the 
Schoenfeld residual plots of the hybrid model.
The evaluation and interpretation of models
The performance of all models was evaluated in the test 
set, and Table 2. presents the Brier scores and C-index 
values for each model. Figure 7 (A) shows the C-index 
values for each RSF and COX model, and Fig. 7 (B) pres­
ents the pairwise statistical comparisons of C-index 
values among the models, with significance levels anno­
tated. To account for multiple comparisons, p-values 
were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.
All models exhibited Brier scores below 0.25, suggest­
ing good calibration. Among the unimodal models, the 
COX-based clinical model achieved the highest C-index 
(0.721), while the RSF-based MRI model performed 
better than the corresponding COX model. Across the 
bimodal models, RSF-based combinations generally 
outperformed COX-based ones. The RSF-based hybrid 
model incorporating CT, MRI, and clinical features 
achieved the best overall performance, with a Brier score 
of 0.101 and a C-index of 0.807 (95% CI: 0.606–0.917), 
significantly outperforming most other models (adjusted 
p < 0.05, Fig. 7). Comparative analysis demonstrated

Based on the optimal risk cutoff (30.49) derived using 
a log-rank–based approach, patients in the test set were 
stratified into low-risk and high-risk groups. Kaplan-
Meier analysis demonstrated a significant difference 
in overall survival between the two groups (log-rank 
p < 0.0001), as shown in Fig. 10. The low-risk group 
exhibited substantially improved survival outcomes com­
pared to the high-risk group, supporting the prognostic 
discriminative ability of the model in a clinical setting.

Discussion
In this study, we developed a multimodal model based on 
Random Survival Forest (RSF) to predict the prognosis 
of pancreatic cancer patients. This model integrates CT 
radiomics features, MRI radiomics features, and clini­
cal characteristics, demonstrating superior performance 
compared to unimodal and bimodal models, as well as 
outperforming the hybrid model built using traditional 
Cox regression. The superiority of the RSF-based hybrid 
model is reflected in its lower Brier score and higher 
C-index, indicating better calibration and discrimination 
ability. Visualization of the model’s feature importance 
reveals that CA125 is the most significant prognostic fac­
tor, followed by AJCC staging, ct_pc2, age, ct_pc1, white 
blood cell count (WBC), and alanine transaminase (ALT). 
These findings suggest that combining radiomic and clin­
ical features in a non-linear model can enhance the accu­
racy of prognosis prediction, offering a more robust tool 
for individualized patient assessment. To further assess 
the clinical utility of the model, patients in the test set 
were stratified into high- and low-risk groups using the 
optimal cutoff of the predicted risk score. The resulting 
Kaplan–Meier curves showed significant survival differ­
ences between groups (p < 0.0001), demonstrating the 
model’s potential for effective risk stratification and per­
sonalized clinical decision-making.
Machine learning, the discipline focused on how 
computers learn from data, has been widely applied to 
clinical datasets for developing robust risk prediction 
models [26, 27]. In recent years, various machine learn­
ing algorithms—such as support vector machines (SVM), 
gradient boosting machines (GBM), and deep neural 
networks—have been explored in medical research for 
classification or regression tasks. However, most of these 
approaches are primarily designed for binary or categori­
cal outcomes and are not directly applicable to time-to-
event data, which often involve censored observations. 
To address this, specialized algorithms have been devel­
oped for survival analysis, including random survival 
forests (RSF), survival support vector machines (survival-
SVM), DeepSurv, and CoxBoost. Among them, RSF, 
first proposed by Ishwaran and colleagues [28], is widely

adopted due to its robustness, non-parametric nature, 
and ability to handle nonlinearities and high-dimensional 
features [29]. RSF applies ensemble learning principles 
to estimate the survival function by aggregating predic­
tions from multiple decision trees built on bootstrap 
samples of the data. In our study, we selected RSF for 
model development because it is well-suited for handling 
continuous survival outcomes and censored data, which 
are essential characteristics of our dataset. As a refer­
ence benchmark, we compared RSF with the traditional 
Cox proportional hazards model, which remains the gold 
standard in clinical survival analysis due to its wide appli­
cation and strong interpretability. Prior studies in vari­
ous cancers—including hepatocellular carcinoma [30], 
colorectal cancer [31], and pancreatic cancer [32]—have 
demonstrated the advantages of RSF over Cox regression. 
Our findings further validate the superior performance of 
RSF in prognostic modeling for pancreatic cancer.
The application of multimodal imaging technology 
shows great potential in predicting tumor phenotyping 
and prognosis. In a study of 50 breast cancer patients, 
Incoronato et al. developed a multivariate model which 
included features extracted from dynamic contrast-
enhanced MRI and SUVmax from PET that correctly 
predicted the tumor molecular subtype (luminal A, lumi­
nal B, HER2, triple-negative) in 77.6% of patients [33]. As 
routine imaging examination approaches, CT and MRI 
are complementary. CT provides clear visualization of 
pancreatic masses and internal structures, particularly 
sensitive to calcifications within tumors, whereas MRI 
excels at soft tissue contrast, offering superior delinea­
tion of tumor margins against adjacent normal pancre­
atic tissue and its involvement with nearby vasculature, 
thus improving the accuracy of tumor staging and local­
ization. Our study combined the radiomics features of 
contrast-enhance CT and MRI to improve data compre­
hensiveness and prediction accuracy, which is less con­
ducted by others.
CA125 is a tumor marker that is widely used in the 
diagnosis and follow-up of many gynecological tumors 
[34], such as cervical cancer and ovarian cancer [35]. 
In fact, CA125 may also be elevated in pancreatic can­
cer, and the utility of CA125 test in the management of 
patients with pancreatic cancer was also evaluated by

several studies [36, 37]. Another study found that CA125 
was the most valuable biomarker to predict the resect­
ability of pancreatic cancer among all the other mark­
ers including CA19-9. Their recent study confirmed that 
elevations of CA125 postoperatively were associated with 
a poor prognosis [38]. Our study shows that CA125 was 
the most important risk factor for poor prognosis in the 
prediction model, which is similar to the studies above.
In contrast with the traditional medical image assess­
ments that mainly focused on tumor size, shape, mar­
gin clarity, contrast enhancement properties, radiomics 
analysis could quantify not only anatomical structure but 
also deeper biological activity such as tumor metabolism, 
angiogenesis, diffusion restriction [39]. Medical imaging 
datasets typically contain a massive amount of pixel or 
voxel information, resulting in high dimensionality. PCA 
aids in reducing this feature space by preserving only the 
principal components that capture the major variance in 
the data, discarding redundant and noise-related infor­
mation, simplifying the dataset, and enhancing subse­
quent analysis efficiency. In this study, ct_pc1 and ct_pc2 
(dimension-reduced contrast-enhanced CT radiomic 
features) showed high importance in the model, indicat­
ing that the radiomics characteristics of the tumor lesion 
area are associated with poor prognosis in pancreatic 
cancer. Fig. S5–7 list the top 10 original features that 
contribute most to these derived radiomic features, rep­
resenting specific imaging traits that influence the prog­
nosis of pancreatic cancer.
There are many factors affecting the prognosis of pan­
creatic cancer, such as TMN stage, tumor specificity, 
body constitution (such as progressive weight loss), etc 
[40, 41]., which make it difficult for clinicians to accu­
rately assess the prognosis. Through the multi-modal 
model in our study, clinicians can make individualized 
treatment plan according to the specific clinical charac­
teristics and imaging features of patients, and improve 
the efficiency of treatment. However, there were still 
some limitations that needed to be raised. First, this was 
a retrospective study with potential selection bias and the 
outcome was limited to overall survival. We expected to 
extend this work to larger cohorts and multicentre stud­
ies with more clinical outcome soon. Second, since our 
patient cohort spans more than a decade, the past his­
tory and treatment information for patients diagnosed 
in earlier years is incomplete. Additionally, in our study, 
not all patients underwent surgical treatment, and many 
pathological reports were obtained through biopsy. As 
a result, data on variables such as microvascular inva­
sion, perineural invasion and surgical margin status are

incomplete. In future studies involving a larger cohort, 
we plan to include only those patients with comprehen­
sive medical and pathological records. Incorporating 
these potential variables will enhance the accuracy and 
robustness of the predictive model. Third, among recent 
studies on prognostic prediction of pancreatic cancer, 
the addition of deep learning techniques has further 
improved the accuracy and reliability of diagnostic and 
predictive results [42, 43]. Compared with traditional 
machine learning algorithms, deep learning techniques 
can transfer and process information through multiple 
neural network layers to capture complex patterns and 
relationships in the data [26, 44]. However, due to the 
small sample size of our study, the use of deep learning 
algorithms is prone to overfitting and poor generaliza­
tion, and our study only used RSF and traditional Cox’s 
proportional risk analysis to develop the models. In the 
future, we look forward to building deep learning-based 
models in a larger study cohort and comparing them with 
traditional machine learning models. Fourth, we did not 
stratify patients according to their risk levels. The imple­
mentation of risk stratification allows physicians to for­
mulate personalized treatment strategies and allocate 
more attention to populations at high risk. The improve­
ment is desirable for future work.
Conclusion
Using the RSF algorithm, a high-performance multi-
modal model based on contrast-enhanced CT and MRI 
was developed. This model facilitates risk stratification 
of patients and holds potential to support individualized 
treatment decision-making. Our research supplemented 
the evidence of radiomics in the prediction of the prog­
nosis of pancreatic cancer patients.

Abstract: Purpose To develop and validate a hybrid radiomics model to predict the overall survival in pancreatic cancer patients and identify risk factors that affect patient prognosis. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 272 pancreatic cancer patients diagnosed at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University from January 2013 to December 2023, and divided them into a training set and a test set at a ratio of 7:3. Pre-treatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images, and clinical features were collected. Dimensionality reduction was performed on the radiomics features using principal component analysis (PCA), and important features with non-zero coefficients were selected using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) with 10-fold cross-validation. In the training set, we built clinical prediction models using both random survival forests (RSF) and traditional Cox regression analysis. These models included a radiomics model based on contrast-enhanced CT, a radiomics model based on MRI, a clinical model, 3 bimodal models combining two types of features, and a multimodal model combining radiomics features with clinical features. Model performance evaluation in the test set was based on two dimensions: discrimination and calibration. In addition, risk stratification was performed in the test set based on predicted risk scores to evaluate the model’s prognostic utility. Results The RSF-based hybrid model performed best with a C-index of 0.807 and a Brier score of 0.101, outperforming the COX hybrid model (C-index of 0.726 and a Brier score of 0.145) and other unimodal and bimodal models. The SurvSHAP(t) plot highlighted CA125 as the most important variable. In the test set, patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups based on the predicted risk scores, and Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated a significant survival difference between the two groups (p < 0.0001). Conclusion A multi-modal model using radiomics based on clinical tabular data and contrast-enhanced CT and MRI was developed by RSF, presenting strengths in predicting prognosis in pancreatic cancer patients.
